# open-consult

An open, Linux-first replacement for Nissan's Consult-I diagnostic tools, built on a
**1998 Nissan Maxima (A32, VQ30DE, 5-speed)** with a cheap FTDI Consult-to-USB cable.
It reads live engine data, reads and clears fault codes, runs active tests, dumps the
engine ROM, and **talks to the body control module**.

## First to crack the IVMS Body Control Module!!!

As far as I can find, **nobody outside Nissan's own CONSULT hand-held has ever
published how to talk to the A32's IVMS body control module.** Every open-source
Consult project in the past and every protocol document stops at the engine ECU. The service manual gives the item names but bytes. 
(Search done 2026-11-15; if you know of earlier work, please tell me and i will credit it.)

Starting from nothing but the service manual and a USB cable, this project:

- **found every Consult unit on the car** by init scan (`ED` engine, `DA` BCM, `DC`
  airbag, `E7` ABS) and identified each one from its part number;
- **worked out BCM command structure**
- **mapped the BCM's 18-byte switch block**: ignition, doors, lock switch, lighting,
  wiper switch and knob, and every power-window switch;
- **drove the body outputs from a laptop**: all four windows, door locks, trunk
  release, hazards, panic, horn + headlights, wipers, rear defogger, interior lamp,
  step lamps and the chime;
- put it all in a GTK app with hold-to-run buttons.

The full write-up is **[`BCM.md`](BCM.md)**, so the next person with an IVMS Nissan
doesn't have to start from zero.

## Also in here

- **Engine ECU, fully probed:** all 73 supported registers with scalings checked on the
  car speed confirmed from gear ratios, the CAS register decoded as a
  crank period, stored codes decoded to OBD-II P-codes, active tests, and a full `C9`
  ROM dump.
- **ROM disassembly** of Mitsubishi 7700: the Consult handler, register
  and active-test tables, fault-code storage, the second CPU, and where the fuel, timing and
  knock maps live. See [`ROM_ANALYSIS.md`](ROM_ANALYSIS.md).
- **Raw logs of every session** in `logs/`, timestamped byte by byte, so every claim in
  the docs can be checked. Logs named `maxine-*` are from the project car; the tools
  name your own logs `YYYY-MM-DD_<test-id>.log`.

## Quick start

```sh
# Python CLI (pyserial). Every run appends a raw TX/RX log to logs/.
python -m consult init                 # engine ECU: FF FF ED -> 12
python -m consult id                   # part number
python -m consult dtc                  # fault codes
python -m consult watch rpm coolant tps speed
python -m consult bcm-watch                # BCM switches, by name
python -m consult bcm-test window-dr-down  # BCM output
python -m consult p1320                    # P1320 monitor
python -m consult knock                    # knock fail-safe state

# GTK 4 app
make && ./consult-gui
```

The cable shows up as a 9600 8N1 serial port (`/dev/ttyUSB0`). Set the FTDI

# Engine ECU ROM analysis: 23710-2L904 (1998 Maxima VQ30DE, M/T)

ROM read over Consult (`rom/23710-2L904_1000-FFFF.bin`), cross-checked against the FSM
and the car. CPU: Mitsubishi 7700 family (M37702-like). Addresses are bank 0.

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [ROM] | Read from code or tables |
| [ROM+car] | Also matches the car |
| [inferred] | Reasoned guess, unchecked |
| [PLMS] | From PLMS's 1999 A32 notes (ECU 23710-4L618, [PDF](https://www.plmsdevelopments.com/files/1999_a32_maxima_obd2_registers.pdf)); unchecked on this ECU |

**Listing:** `rom/23710-2L904.asm` is generated from `tools/m7700dis.py` and the
annotation file `rom/23710-2L904.ann`. Edit the `.ann`, then regenerate:
`python3 tools/m7700dis.py rom/23710-2L904_1000-FFFF.bin --ann rom/23710-2L904.ann -o rom/23710-2L904.asm`.

## 1. Consult handler (serial ISR `consult_isr`, `$4EF5`; reply builder `consult_task`, `$996A`) [ROM]

- **Init:** `FF FF` then only **`ED`** is accepted (`CMPB #$ED` at `$4FAE`). The reply
  is the complement, `12`. Any other ID byte drops back to waiting for `FF`. ECUTalk's
  `EF` never works on this ECU.
- **Accepted command bytes:** `FF` (re-init), `30` (stop), `C9` (memory read, 2 address
  bytes), `5A` (register, 1 byte), `0A` (active test), `D0`, `D1`, `C1`, and **`51`**.
  Anything else gets `FE` back. This matches the car (3.2: unsupported = `A5 FE`).
- **`51` is undocumented:** on `F0` it reports the "seen this ignition cycle" flags
  (`$0810–$0822`) as codes and clears them. It also zeroes test state (`$0E51–$0E57`,
  `$0E78–$0E7A`). Confirmed and pending codes are untouched, but avoid sending it
  until it has been tried on purpose.
- **`5A`:** register numbers `00–61` only (`CMPB #$62`). The RAM address comes from the
  pointer table at `$1000` (2 bytes per register, `$FFFF` = unsupported).
- **Request limit:** a new `5A`/`C9` is refused (`FE`) once the argument buffer
  (`$08D2`, counter `$073B`) holds `$28` = 40 bytes. `5A` stores 1 byte per register and
  `C9` 2 per address, so up to **40 registers** or 20 addresses per request. That is
  more than the usual "20 registers" (checklist 3.3), and untested on the car.
- **`0A <t> <v>`:** `t` in `80–AD` looks up a 2-byte descriptor at `$1160+2(t−80)`
  (§4). A first byte below `08` selects a separate "direct" mode that loads a stream
  list from tables at `$EA3F`/`$EA5B`. It is probably the OBD Mode 6 test results:
  the pointers come in sets that match the FSM's TID list. [inferred]
- **`C9` on `$5D40–$623F` is forwarded to the second processor (§6), so the ROM dump
  has a 1.25 KB hole.** For those addresses the reply builder (`$9AEB`) doesn't read
  this CPU's memory (nor `$FE00–$FFCF` when config bit `$1207.5` is set; it's clear
  here). `$543F` queues each one as address − `$5000`. The request goes to the other CPU
  through the shared RAM (`$024C/$024E`), and its answer (`$02B6` → `$07E7`) is put into
  the reply **one byte per frame, from the second frame on**. Our `rom-dump` read one
  frame per request, so **our dump of `$5D40–$623F` is stale reply bytes, not ROM**. It
  repeats the last good block, except for one varying byte per block, probably the
  other CPU's data. This CPU's own code there (the scheduler calls `$5F1B`) can only be
  read off the chip (checklist 11.2). The listing marks the range as a hole. `python -m
  consult sub-dump` streams each address to read the **other CPU's** `$0D40–$123F`
  (untested).
- **`D0`** returns the 32 bytes at ROM `$11C0` verbatim (they match the car byte for
  byte). The last 5 are ASCII `2L904`. The middle bytes are **not** a bitmap of
  supported registers or tests (checked). ASCII `J8ZM06` at `$FFCA` looks like the
  calibration ID.

## 2. Register map (`5A`), from the table at `$1000` [ROM]

73 supported registers, which is exactly the set the car scan found. Scalings are from
the car (checklist §3).

| Reg | RAM | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `00`/`01` | `$0995`/`$0994` | RPM, word × 12.5 [ROM+car] |
| `02`/`03` | `$097A`/`$0979` | **Period of the 120° REF signal**, not RPM. Copied from captured timer value `$A8`. At 1175–1188 rpm, word × rpm = 2.49 M; at 2400–2600 rpm, 2.50 M (word ≈ 1005). A 120° signal with an 8 µs timer tick predicts exactly 2.5 M. So **rpm ≈ 2 500 000 / word**. [ROM+car] |
| `04`/`05` | `$09D6`/`$09D5` | MAF, × 5 mV |
| `08` | `$0980` | Coolant, − 50 °C |
| `09` / `0A` | `$0B18` / `$0B36` | Front O2 sensors, × 10 mV. FSM: on the A32, **B1 = right bank, B2 = left bank** |
| `0B` | `$098B` | Vehicle speed, × 2 km/h |
| `0C` | `$09F4` | Battery, × 80 mV |

## 3. Fault codes [ROM+car]

### 3.1 How codes are stored

- 152 fault slots, each a bit in five 19-byte arrays (bit `$80` first):

  | Array | Meaning | Set by |
  |---|---|---|
  | `$0580` | **1st-trip (pending)** | `dtc_detect` (`$DE86`) on the first trip |
  | `$05A0` | **Confirmed** (MIL) | `dtc_confirm` (`$D371`) on the 2nd trip |
  | `$05C0` | Confirmed at some point (history) | `dtc_confirm` |
  | `$0810` | Detected this ignition cycle | both |
  | `$0830` | 1st-trip already handled this cycle | `dtc_detect` |

- **`D1`/`C1` reply** (`$99DF`): confirmed codes first, each with its starts counter
  (a code drops out of the reply once its counter reaches 40), then **1st-trip codes,
  each with the starts byte hard-coded `F5`**. No codes gives `55 00`. This confirms
  the "`F5` = pending" reading from checklist 2.6. **`C1`** builds the same reply and
  only then requests the clear, so the reply shows the codes as they were before the
  clear (as seen on the car).
- Slot *i* is reported by `D1` as the byte at **`$9E0E + i`**. That table simply runs
  `11–18, 21–28, … E1–E8, 19–1F, 10, 29–2F, 20, …`, so the code byte is an index, not
  a Nissan code number.
- Slot *i*'s OBD-II code is the BCD word at **`$E086 + 2i`** (e.g. `04 43` = P0443).
  Pointers to per-slot counters are at `$E1C6 + 2i`.
- 123 slots have a P-code. **All 86 DTCs in the FSM index are among them**, which
  checks the mapping. The other 37 are generic slots this firmware shares with other
  Nissan engines (P0235 turbo, P0307/P0308, …).
- `consult/dtcs.py` and `src/registers.c` are generated from these tables plus the FSM
  names. The script is reproducible: read the two tables and join on *i*.

### 3.2 This car's codes, decoded

| `D1` byte | P-code | FSM name | ECM Mode II code | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `21` | **P1320** | IGN SIGNAL-PRIMARY | 0201 | Returns within seconds of a clear. FSM causes: harness/connectors, coil power transistors, **condenser** (> 1 MΩ across its terminals at 25 °C), CKP (REF) sensor and circuit |
| `34` | **P0325** | KNOCK SEN/CIRCUIT | 0304 | One-trip logic, no MIL, no freeze frame (FSM). Signal is ECM terminal 64, 2.0–3.0 V at idle. |
| `A8` | **P0443** | PURG VOLUME CONT/V | 1008 | EVAP canister purge volume control valve circuit. A 4-phase stepper on ECM terminals 26, 27, 110, 118 (EC-282). |

After a clear, `21` and `A8` return with starts byte `F5`: 1st-trip (pending), MIL off
[ROM+car]. A detection on a later trip confirms them.

### 3.3 Freeze frame (`$DC62`)

When a fault confirms, the ECU writes the P-code to `$05E2` (registers `3B/3C`), then
copies `$0C4C` (first read as load; it is a 00/FF flag, §2), `$0985`, `$0869/$086A`, fuel-trim values (`$0B5A`, `$0B44`,
`$0B2E` / 200) and a speed value into `$05E4–$05ED`. The FSM's freeze-frame item list
(fuel system status ×2, CAL/LD, coolant, short/long fuel trim ×2, RPM, speed) fits.
The exact order is still to confirm by reading `3B–47` on the car.

## 4. Active tests (`0A`), descriptor table at `$1160` [ROM]

Descriptor `(mask, ctl)`: `ctl >> 4` picks a flag byte `$07AC+n` (copied to `$07B7+n`
on `F0`). `(ctl & 7F) >> 1` is the value slot (`$076F + slot`). Every test takes a
value byte. Any running test sets `$07F1.2` (sent to the second CPU). Handlers marked
"bank 1" aren't readable over Consult (§8).

| Test | Flag | Value | Handler | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `80` | `$07B7.01` | `$076F` | bank 1 | Coolant temp override |
| `81` | `$07B7.02` | `$0770` | `$6E15`, `$7434` | **Fuel injection**: clamped `4B–7D` (75–125 %), written into alpha `$0730` |
| `82` | `$07B7.04` | `$0771` | bank 1 | Ignition timing |
| `85` | `$07B7.20` | `$0774` | `$ACB3` | **IACV-AAC opening**: forces register `18`, ≤ `81` steps |
| `88` | `$07B8.01` | `$0777` | bank 1 | Power balance (cylinder 1 cut on the car) |
| `89` | `$07B8.02` | `$0778` | bank 1 | Fuel pump relay |
| `8B` | `$07B8.08` | `$077A` | bank 1 | Self-learning clear |
| `8C` | `$07B8.10` | `$077B` | `$ACA0` | Forces an idle-air path (`$BC22`, constant `$22AF`) |
| `93` / `94` | `$07B9.08/.10` | `$0782/3` | bank 1 | Cooling fan low / high (fan ran on the car). Use as a pair |
| `95` | `$07B9.20` | `$0784` | bank 1 | ? |
| `98` | `$07BA.01` | `$0787` | `$BFB3`, `$7384` | **PURG VOL CONT** *(inferred, strong)*: forces register `29`, limit `$26BC` |
| `99` | `$07BA.02` | `$0788` | bank 1 | ? |
| `9A` | `$07BA.04` | `$0789` | bank 1 | Canister vent control valve [PLMS] |
| `9C` | `$07BA.10` | `$078B` | bank 1 | Vacuum cut bypass valve [PLMS] |
| `A2` | `$07BB.04` | `$0791` | `$F4C0` | On/off (value 0 / non-0): forces output bit `$095D.2` in task `$F468`, which otherwise switches it on throttle (`37`) and speed thresholds `$2BBC–$2BBE`. Engine mount? *(inferred, weak)* |
| `A6` | `$07BB.40` | `$0795` | bank 1 | ? |
| `A7` | `$07BB.80` | `$0796` | bank 1 | Vacuum cut bypass valve [PLMS] |
| `AA` | `$07BC.04` | `$0799` | `$5406` | **Persistent side effect:** stopping it sets backup-RAM `$0F69.4`, which stops the session reset (`$550A`) from clearing `$0F69` bits 7–6. Bit 7 gates logic at `$9DEF`. Avoid |
| `AB` | `$07BC.08` | `$079A` | `$98BB`, `$992E` | Drives a backup-RAM monitor sequence (`$0F6C–$0F6E`, uses register `3A`); canister vent valve [PLMS] |
| `AC` | `$07BC.10` | `$079B` | bank 1 | ? |
| `AD` | `$07BC.20` | `$079C` | bank 1 | ? |

- `$511D` rejects tests outside `80`–`AD`. **Don't fire unknown tests**: on a 1999 ECU
  one above `9F` re-registered the NATS keys [PLMS].
- Fans [PLMS]: low = `93 01` + `94 00`, high = `93 00` + `94 01`. Both `01`: avoid.
- `83` has code (`$B39A`) but no descriptor, so it's rejected.

## 5. Interrupts (from what each handler writes)

| Vector | Handler | Role |
|---|---|---|
| INT2 | `$4797` | **Crank REF (120°) edge**: captures the REF period (registers `02/03`) and builds the coil-fire mask `$0A0C` [ROM]. The old listing called this "knock". |
| Timer A3 | `$4495` | Fires the coils in `$0A0C` [inferred] |
| Timer A2 | `$46C0` | Dispatches on event flags `$B9` (crank POS / timing events?) |
| UART0 TX | `$4BC2` | Used as the periodic **scheduler tick**: runs the task list (sensor reads, fuel, ignition, idle, diagnostics, `consult_task`) |
| UART1 RX + TX | `$4EF5` | Consult |
| Timer A4, B2 | `$4540`, `$44B6` | **Knock interface chip**: per-cylinder values to `$030266`; B2 also runs the chip watchdog (§8b) |
| NMI | `$473F` | Not verified |

The Consult code uses registers `$32/$35/$36` (data out, status, data in) and `$F0/$F1`
(enables). That doesn't fit the stock M37702 register map, so the exact chip variant
is unconfirmed; read the markings when the ECU is out (checklist 11.3).

## 6. Second processor and the shared RAM at `$0200–$02FF` [ROM]

This ECU has a second CPU (or another bus master), linked by an 8-bit shared RAM at
`$0200–$02FF`. Every access uses either even or odd addresses only, which fits an
8-bit chip on one byte lane. Nothing in this ROM writes the incoming half, but the
code reads it constantly.

- **Outgoing** (`obd_task`, `$CC52`): RPM, load, trims, purge step, timing, CAL/LD,
  speed, battery, switch/output bits and the pending `C9` address, written to
  `$0202, $0204, … $025E`. `$029E` is the handshake: `A5` means the other side is ready.
- **Incoming:** `$02A0–$02FE`, picked up by `$C7F5` according to the message type in
  `$029E & 7`. Type 0 carries the **fault-detection flags `$0E51–$0E58`**, which
  `$D1E8`/`$D237` turn into `dtc_detect` calls. Those cover slots 48–95 (misfire
  P0300–P0306, catalyst, EVAP, **P0443**, A/T…) and, through `$0E58`, front O2, EGR,
  IAT and others. Other types fill values such as `$088E–$0892` and `$0829–$082B`.
- **So many OBD-II monitors, including the one that set P0443, run on the other CPU**,
  whose code we don't have. It probably also handles the GST (OBD-II) line on ECM pin
  69 [inferred]. Its memory should be readable through the `C9` forward (§1).
- The write-only window `$38xx–$3Bxx` (143 writes, no reads) gets copies of DTC,
  freeze-frame and `C9` request values. It may be a second output path or a debug
  port [unknown].

## 7. How this car's codes are detected

- **P1320 (`21`, slot 8)** at `$E2F6` [ROM+car]: fixed-rate slow task (`$4C69`), not
  synced to ignition. Enabled by `$120C.7`.

  | Step | Code | Detail |
  |---|---|---|
  | Preconditions | `$E2F6–$E328` | `$0850.0`, not `$07EE.5`, REF valid (`$092A.6`, `$0931.2`), past start or `$0ACA` ≥ 30, load `$09AE` ≥ 4. Else count = 0 |
  | Spacing | `$0C6F` | Sample needs ≥ 2; a miss resets it. ≤ 1 miss per 2 calls |
  | Sample | `$E331` | P4.3 (`$0A.3`) high = miss |
  | Count | `$0C60` | +1 per miss, sets `$0811.7` |
  | Detect | `$E341` | At 10: `dtc_detect(8)`, count back to 0 |

  | Drive (655 s) | |
  |---|---|
  | Detections | 2–5 per second; never 0.15 s without a miss |
  | Misses | 18–20/s idle, 42–48/s under load (near the ceiling) |
  | P4.3 high | 36 % at `$09AE` 32–63, 92 % at ≥ 224; 0 KOEO |

  P4.3 has no FSM wire of its own (EC-331 … 333); presumably an internal check on the
  six coil outputs (pins 1 2 3 7 8 9) [inferred]. All cylinders fire, so the *check*
  fails. A ~11 ms window per spark on every cylinder fits the numbers, which points at a
  shared cause: condenser, coil supply or ground, coil type, or the ECM [inferred].
- **P0325 (`34`, slot 19)**: not set in bank 0; probably by the second CPU, which gets
  knock-chip timeouts via `$0235` (§8b) [inferred].

## 8. Calibration maps [ROM + PLMS]

Same layout as PLMS's 1999 ECU: every address holds the table PLMS names. The code
that reads them isn't traced (no direct operands or pointers found).

| Address | Size | Table | What our ROM shows there |
|---|---|---|---|
| `$1220` | 128 | VQ (MAF voltage → flow) | Rising 16-bit words `0003 000E 0021 003D …` |
| `$1400` | 16×16 | Volumetric efficiency | First row `7A`–`7D` |
| `$1500` / `$1510` | 16 | VE load / rpm scale | `08 10 … 80` / `10 20 … FF` |
| `$1700` | 16×16 | Fuel map | `80` (= 100 %?) rising to `AE` |
| `$1800` | 16×16 | **Knock** fuel map | Same shape, lower at high load (row 15: `A5` vs `AE`) |
| `$1900` / `$1910` | 16 | Fuel load / rpm scale | `08 10 … 80` |
| `$19A0` | 16 | After-start enrichment vs temperature | `6F 6F 55 42 32 … 0B`, falls with temperature |
| `$19C0` | 16 | Cold-start enrichment vs temperature | `58 … 48` |
| `$1D00` | 16×16 | **Ignition timing** | Rows 9–15: plain degrees, 48° falling to 13° across the row. Rows 1–8, columns 7–15: bit 7 set, low 7 bits plausible degrees (`9E` → 30°); the flag's meaning is open |
| `$1E00` | 16×16 | **Knock** timing map | Same, but up to ~9° lower in most high-load cells (161 of 256 cells lower) |
| `$1F00` / `$1F10` | 16 | Timing rpm / load scale | `08 10 … 40 44 48 …` / `08 10 … 80` |

Row/column axes need the lookup code. Measured WOT timing to compare against: 9–10°
at 3750–4500 rpm, 15–16° above 5000 (checklist 3.14).

**Bank 1:** the firmware calls 24 routines at `$01xxxx` (e.g. `$4C96 $4CEE $4CF2 $4D20
$4D52`). `C9` takes 16-bit addresses, so they need a chip read. Nothing in bank 0 points
at the 2D maps, so their lookups are there. 1D lookups (`interp8/16/32`, `$EA77`) are in
bank 0.

Timing path in bank 0 (INT2, `$47A8`):

| Term | RAM | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base timing | `$0BA6` | Set only at reset in bank 0; the map value from bank 1 [inferred] |
| Knock retard | `$0DB7/$0DB8` | §8b. Ignored if `$28AC` ≠ 0 (here `00`) |
| Correction | `$0E01` | `$A9B9`, from `$0DFC` and the knock retard |
| Correction | `$096D` | `interp8` of table `$2270` by `$09B0`, only under conditions (`$5694`) |
| Limits | `$20D7/$20D8`, `$20D4` | Clamp, then target `$0BA8` = `$20D4` − sum, clamped `30–75` |
| Rate limit | `$0BA9` | Steps toward `$0BA8` by at most `$0BAA` (advance) / `$20D5` (retard) |
| Per-cylinder | `$0DB0–$0DB5` | Subtracted per cylinder; register `16` = `$0BA9` − trim + `80` (`$4928`) |


## 8b. Knock control [ROM]


| Part | Where | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Knock interface chip | bank 3 I/O: `$030262` control, `$030266` data | Programmed per cylinder from the Timer A4 / B2 interrupts (`$4545`, `$44C4`). Self-test handshake at `$9EDA`: reads `CC00` → chip OK (`$0DD0.0`, `.6`); `AA55` → reply `55AA` |
| Per-cylinder values | 6 × 16-word tables `$26F0–$2790` (normal), `$27B0–$2850` (alternate) | Indexed by `$09AC` (rpm-related) into `$0DE1–$0DEB`, sent to the chip per cylinder (`$4579`). `FFFF` outside the active rpm band. Alternate set is flat (`0025–0028`) and used when `$0DCF.3` is set |
| Chip watchdog | Timer B2, `$44E8` | If the second CPU's `$021F.3` doesn't toggle for `$239F` interrupts: clear `$0DD0.0` (chip not OK), pulse `$0710.0` → `$0235` to the second CPU, count in `$0DE0` |
| Knock status | `$0213.3` (from the second CPU) | 1 = knock system OK |
| Active zone | `$9F27–$9FA8` | Coolant ≥ `$2883` (60 °C), REF valid, not cranking, rpm index `$09B1` ≥ `$2881`, CAL/LD `$0ABE` ≥ `$2882` (56 %), with hysteresis. Outside it the retard is cleared |
| Retard | `$0DC1` → `$0DB7/8` | `$2884` per knock event (`$0DC7` = count from the interrupt); learned separately below / above rpm index `$2880` (`$0DB9`, `$0DBB`); slewed by `$288E`; clamped to `$0DD1/$0DD3` |
| **Fail-safe** | `$9FBC–$9FE2` | If `$0213.3` = 0 (or `$0DD0.7`): latch `$070D.7`, set **fixed retard `$2895` = `FC`** (−4 counts, i.e. 4° less advance in register-16 units *(inferred)*), set `$0DCF.3` (alternate tables) |

**This car (P0325 stored):** probably in fail-safe, ~4° fixed retard [inferred]. Check:
`python -m consult knock`.

2. Knock fail-safe state (§8b): `python -m consult knock`.
3. Chip read: bank 1 (maps, test handlers) and `$5D40–$623F`.
4. Dump the second CPU with `sub-dump`.
5. Confirm the [PLMS] scalings on a drive; name `28 2A 3A 60`.
6. Unknown active tests `95 99 A6 AC AD` (bank 1). Don't fire them.
7. Decode `D0` bytes 0–26.

## assistant 2026-11-15T18:50:56.822Z

I found two live adjustments you can make over Consult: a global fuel multiplier and an ignition timing offset. There's no way to change the actual maps or poke values into RAM from the cable.

**1. You can't write to RAM over Consult.** The Consult handler in the ROM (`consult_isr`, `rom/23710-2L904.asm:3308`) only accepts `FF`, `30`, `C9`, `5A`, `0A`, `D0`, `D1`, `C1` and `51`. `C9` only reads memory. There is a hidden hook at `$4EFA` that jumps into bank 1 if config bit `$1206.0` is set, but that bit is in ROM and it's clear. So you can't poke values into RAM or redirect anything.

**2. The maps are in ROM, not RAM.** The fuel map (`$1700`), timing map (`$1D00`), their knock versions (`$1800`, `$1E00`), the VE table and the MAF curve are all fixed in the chip (ROM_ANALYSIS §8). The code that looks them up is in bank 1, which we haven't read yet. A real per-cell tune means reprogramming or replacing the chip, which needs the ECU out and a look at the board (that's already checklist 11.2/11.3).

**3. Active tests are the live knobs.**

- **`81` fuel injection, 75–125 %.** I traced this one (`$6E15` → `$7434`). The value goes straight into alpha, the fuel correction that normally follows the O2 sensors, for both banks (`$0730`/`$0731`). So it scales all fuelling at once; you can't trim individual load or rpm cells.
  - While it's held, the O2 feedback and learning stop. It's a fixed multiplier.
  - The only check I found in the readable code is whether the test is active. Nothing there cancels it above some rpm or speed.
  - It stays on as long as the session keeps streaming. If the cable drops, the ECU times out after `$80` ticks (`$996F`), clears the tests and goes back to stock. That's a reasonable fail-safe.
  - I haven't confirmed it still applies at wide-open throttle. Check on the car: watch the injector pulse width (registers `14`/`15`) at a steady load with `81` at `64` (100 %), then at a higher value.
- **`82` ignition timing.** Its handler is in bank 1, so I don't know how far it can go or whether it works under load. Your CLI caps it at ±5°.
- **`80` coolant override.** This would change the cold-start enrichment, but faking coolant temperature is a bad way to tune.
- Any running test also sets a status bit (`$DA97`) and flag `$07F1.2` for the second CPU. That probably pauses the OBD monitors while the test runs (inferred).

**The practical route** is to use `81` and `82` to measure what the engine wants, then put those numbers into a reprogrammed chip. The stock O2 sensors can't measure air-fuel ratio at full throttle, so you need a wideband sensor and gauge first. Leaning out at wide-open throttle without one is how pistons get melted. Have a second person run the laptop, or do it on a dyno, not while you're driving.

Your CLI currently limits `fuel-trim` to ±10 % (`consult/__main__.py:468`). I can add a mode that holds a fuel/timing setting while logging rpm, load, injector pulse and timing (plus a wideband if you have one), so you can map it cell by cell. Want that?

## assistant 2026-11-15T18:52:32.558Z

Probably with a chip programmer once the ECU is out. I don't see a way to do it over Consult.

**Why Consult can't reach it.** The `C9` reply builder (`$9AF1`) reads with `LDA $00,X`. That's a 16-bit address, so the bank comes from the CPU's data-bank register. The only places that set it are the reset vector (`$3D80`) and the handler for unused interrupts (`$4486`), and both set it to `00`. Nothing in bank 0 ever sets it to 1. If some bank 1 routine set it to 1 and the Consult task interrupted it, a `C9` read would land in bank 1. But bank 1 code most likely uses long (24-bit) addresses, and we can't check that without reading it. Consult also has no write command, so I can't plant a pointer for the firmware to follow. Bank 1 is not reachable from the cable.

**Why I think it's on a separate chip.** The firmware talks to the knock chip at `$030262`/`$030266`, which is bank 3. That means the CPU runs with an external address/data bus. The shared RAM at `$0200` and the write-only `$38xx` window also look like external hardware. So bank 1 is probably a separate parallel ROM, something like a 128 KB 27C010 or 28F010, on that bus. It may even hold all the code, with bank 0 just the first half. That's an inference until we see the board.

**Plan:**
1. **Pull the ECU and photograph both sides of the board.** Read the markings on the CPU (M377xx plus suffix), any 28/32-pin DIP or PLCC/TSOP memory chip, and any daughterboard header. This step decides everything else.
2. **If there's an external ROM or flash** (most likely):
   - Read it with a cheap programmer (TL866II or T48), either with a clip in-circuit or desoldered. In-circuit only works if the CPU stops driving the bus, e.g. held in reset, which isn't guaranteed. Desoldering is the safer read.
   - Check the image against our 60 KB `C9` dump to work out the layout. The same image also fills the `$5D40–$623F` hole.
   - If it's desoldered, put a socket in. You can then plug in an EPROM emulator (Moates Ostrich-style) and **edit the real maps live while the engine runs**. That's the per-cell tuning you asked about earlier, which Consult can't give you.
3. **If the CPU's internal mask ROM holds the code and there's no external memory:** this is much harder. Internal fetches never appear on the bus, so watching the bus with a logic analyser shows nothing. You'd be into chip-specific test-mode tricks or decapping. If the board shows this, I'd look for other people's dumps of the same part number first.

**What we can learn from the car meanwhile:**
- Read `$FFxx` and check where the bank 1 `JSL` targets (`$0170B5`, `$017B08`, …) fall, to guess how big bank 1 is.
- Look at the reset code's processor-mode setup (`$5E`/`$5F`-area writes) for memory-expansion or microprocessor mode.

Once you've got the ECU out, send me the board photos and I'll pin down which case it is.

| Part | Likely role |
|---|---|
| Large QFP top-left (by the crystal) | Main 7700 CPU — the one we dumped |

| Large QFP top-right `…2S1AFM1…` (own crystal) | Unknown — possibly the second CPU |
| PLCC-84 sticker `KNKT43J` | Hitachi H8 ZTAT (OTP). The second/knock processor from §6 |
| 2× Mitsubishi `M5955?FP` SOP | Output drivers, not memory |
| Unpopulated 2-row header across the top | Factory test / emulator header |

One caveat: those filenames look like Photobucket forum images. Confirm the label on this ECU reads 23710-2L904 before trusting the layout.

Given mask-ROM internal code, the realistic paths are:

1. **Find an existing full image.** Mask-ROM Nissans of this era get reprogrammed by plugging a board into that top header and switching the CPU to run from external ROM — which needs a complete image, bank 1 included. If any aftermarket tuning board supports this ECU family, someone already has that dump. Worth searching before extracting anything yourself. If one exists, it's also your route to real per-cell map tuning, since `$1700`/`$1D00` are just data in it.
2. **Read the H8 (`KNKT43J`).** ZTAT parts have a PROM read mode via a PLCC-84 adapter (unpowered clip or desolder). Doesn't get bank 1, but it holds the §6 monitor code — the stuff behind P0443 and misfire detection — which we have zero visibility into today.
3. **Map the header pinout.** ECU unpowered, continuity-beep each header pin to the main CPU's bus/RESET/CNVss/BYTE pins. That tells us what processor modes the board supports and whether the external-ROM route is even wired.

So: for live tuning, `81`/`82` over Consult remain your only in-car knobs. For map editing you need a full ROM image, and the most practical way to get one is to find an existing community dump of this family rather than extract the mask ROM yourself.

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:05:43.228Z

I went through every Consult command path for a memory-safety or logic hole that would widen read access. Here's the honest result.

## Nothing found that gets you further than you already are

**`C9` already reads the entire readable address space.** I traced the bounds logic in `consult_reply_c9` (`$9AF1`) and confirmed the config bytes from the ROM:

- `$1206 = 00` → the ISR's bank-1 debug hook at `$4EFA` (jump to `$017B08`) is **off**.
- `$1207 = 52` → bit 5 clear, so the `$FE00–$FFCF` hiding is **off**. `C9` reads those addresses normally.

So `C9` returns all of `$1000–$FFFF` **except `$5D40–$623F`** (the second-CPU forward). Your 61 KB dump already spans `FExx`, so there's no free ROM being left on the table.

## Why the two real gaps are hardware, not a defeatable check

- **Bank 1 (`$01xxxx`: the 2D-map lookups, bank-1 test handlers).** `C9`'s read is `LDA $00,X` — a 16-bit address in the data-bank register. Bank-0 code sets that register to `00` only (`$3D80`, `$4486`) and never changes it. There's no software gate to bypass; the address simply can't be formed. Matches §8c: bank 1 is internal mask ROM.
- **`$5D40–$623F` (this CPU's real code).** The skip at `$9AFB–$9B03` is a pure address-range compare with no attacker-controlled input. Can't be steered.

## The one config-gated backdoor can't be reached

`$1206.0` would route the Consult ISR into bank 1 — a genuine entry point. But it's a **ROM/calibration byte**, not RAM, so it's read-only at runtime anyway, and I found **no write primitive** to flip anything:

- `5A` stores a register index that's validated `< 0x62` and resolved through the fixed ROM pointer table at `$1000` (`$9BB0`).
- `0A` stores the test value at `$076F + at_slot`, where `at_slot` comes from the ROM descriptor, not the wire.
- `C9` stores only addresses into `cs_argbuf`.

None take an attacker-chosen destination, so you can't poke RAM, let alone ROM config.

## The one actual bug — and why it doesn't help

The arg-count limit (`CMP #$28; BCS reject`, `$53BF`) is checked only when a *new* `5A`/`C9` command byte arrives, not between the two bytes of a `C9` address. So: send 39× `5A` (argc→39, still `< 40`), then one `C9` — it's accepted, then collects 2 bytes unchecked, pushing `argc` to 41 and writing one byte past the 40-byte `cs_argbuf` (`$08D2`). The reply loop then reads ~2 bytes beyond the buffer and interprets them as an extra address.

But that extra address is still a bank-0 address read with data-bank 0 — i.e. memory `C9` already reads directly. It's a latent off-by-one, not an access-widener.

## Bottom line

The handler is tight for this purpose. The only *under-used* intended capability is `sub-dump` (the `$5D40–$623F` forward → the second CPU's `$0D40–$123F`), which is a different chip, not bank 1. Getting bank 1 still means silicon: find a community full image for the 4L6xx family, or read the `KNKT43J` H8 — exactly §8c.

Want me to add a short "§10 Consult attack surface (audited, no escalation found)" to `ROM_ANALYSIS.md` recording this, so nobody re-walks it?

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:09:23.504Z

I chased exactly that angle, and it closes off for a concrete structural reason. Three things I checked:

**1. The overflow byte lands in dead RAM.** Reset's RAM-clear loop runs `LDX #$08F9` downward (`$3DAD`), so it initializes up to `$08F9` — the last real `cs_argbuf` byte — and leaves `$08FA–$08FF` untouched. And grep for any access to `$08FA–$08FF` is **empty**: nothing in the ROM ever reads that region. So the one byte we can write past the buffer corrupts no pointer, no variable, nothing. It's padding.

**2. The read-back is still a bank-0 address.** When the reply loop runs off the end, it reads `$08FA` (our controlled byte, as the high byte) and `$08FB` (stale dead RAM, low byte) and treats them as one address `$XX??`. It then does `LDA $00,X` on it — a 16-bit read in data bank 0. So you get a half-controlled read of memory `C9` already reaches in full. No new region.

**3. Nothing in this ECU can form a bank-1 address from data, by construction.** This is the real wall. To read `$01xxxx` you'd need one of two things, and the ROM has neither in any Consult-reachable path — or anywhere:

- **Data-bank register ≠ 0.** The only `LDT` instructions in the entire image are `LDT #$00` at `$3D80` (reset) and `$4486` (unused-IRQ). DT is *never* set to anything but 0, anywhere. (The `PHB`/`PLB` at `$513A`/`$5156` are push/pull of accumulator B, not the bank register, and they restore the same value.)
- **A long/indirect read `LDA [dp],Y`** whose pointer carries a bank byte. Grep for `LDA [` / `LDB [` / long-indirect is **empty** — the firmware never uses 24-bit indirection. The only indirect loads at all are `LDA ($00,X)` in the DTC path and a fixed `JMP ($CBAB,X)` table, both 16-bit, bank 0, and neither takes a Consult argument.

So an indirect read is exactly what's missing. For the overflow to reach bank 1 it would have to corrupt a pointer that some *later* code dereferences with a bank byte — but (a) the byte goes to dead RAM, and (b) no such bank-crossing dereference exists to aim at. The data-bank register being a hard `0` everywhere is what makes bank 1 unreachable by any software trick, not just by the `C9` range check.

It was the right thing to poke at — it's the one genuine memory-safety bug on the surface — but it bottoms out in unused RAM with no indirection behind it.

Want me to tighten §10's "no payoff" line with these two concretes (`$08FA` is uncleared/unread dead RAM; `LDT` is `#$00` at the only two sites, no long-indirect anywhere)?

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:11:54.398Z

Both leads are recorded in §10. Here's where the hunt stands after chasing every thread.

## Verdict: no software path to bank 1 — and now I can say *why*, concretely

I set out to find any one of three primitives that could widen access. Each is provably absent from Consult's reach:

| Primitive you'd need | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Bank-crossing read** (DT≠0 or `[dp]` long-indirect) | Absent everywhere | `LDT` is `#$00` at the only two sites; zero long-indirect loads in the image |
| **Arbitrary write** (caller-chosen destination) | Absent | `5A`→validated ROM table; `0A`→fixed slot in `$076F–$079C`; `C9`→`cs_argbuf` only |
| **Code execution** (corruptible RAM pointer) | Absent | Only one indirect jump in the ROM, through a fixed ROM table with a bounded ROM index; no RAM function pointers at all |

And the one genuine memory-safety bug — the `cs_argbuf` off-by-one — deposits its single controlled byte at `$08FA`, which reset never clears and **no code ever reads**. It corrupts nothing. The read it induces is a bank-0 address formed with data bank 0, i.e. memory `C9` already dumps in full.

The config-gated backdoor (`$1206.0` → ISR jumps into bank 1) is real but doubly out of reach: the bit lives in ROM, and there's no write primitive to flip RAM even if it lived there.

So this isn't "I didn't find it yet" — it's a closed result. The interface is a bounded read + narrow write diagnostic by construction. Bank 1 is internal mask ROM and the firmware never exposes a lever to leave bank 0.

## Where the energy should actually go

Since software escalation is out, the realistic routes to bank 1 (all in §8c):

1. **A community full image for the 4L6xx family** — your photographed '99 is 23710-4L618, the exact ECU PLMS's map addresses come from. If any aftermarket tuning board supports it, a complete dump already exists. Best effort/reward by far.
2. **Read the `KNKT43J` H8** (PLCC-84 ZTAT, PROM mode) — gets you the §6 second-CPU monitor code, which is a real gap, even though it isn't bank 1.
3. **Chip read of the main CPU** — only if 1–2 fail; mask-ROM internal read is the hard, invasive case.

One thing I *can* squeeze out in software that's under-used today: `sub-dump` pulls the second CPU's `$0D40–$123F` through the `$5D40–$623F` forward. Want me to run/verify that path's decode next, or branch and commit §8c + §10 as they stand?

def cmd_sub_dump(c, args):
    """C9 on the range the ECU forwards to its second processor (ROM_ANALYSIS.md §6).

    For C9 addresses $5D40-$623F the ECU doesn't read its own memory: it passes
    (address - $5000) to the other CPU and fills the byte from that CPU's reply, one
    per frame, starting with the second frame. So each address is streamed for
    `--frames` frames and the value is kept only when the later frames agree.
    Read-only. Output: rom/sub_<first-5000>-<last-5000>.bin and a .txt of each
    address's frames, so unstable bytes can be checked.
    """
    connect(c)
    first, last = args.first, args.last
    os.makedirs(ROM_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    base = os.path.join(ROM_DIR, f"sub_{first - 0x5000:04X}-{last - 0x5000:04X}")
    data, unstable, t0 = bytearray(), 0, time.monotonic()
    with open(base + ".txt", "w") as txt:
        for addr in range(first, last + 1):
            frames = []
            try:
                c.command(bytes([0xC9, addr >> 8, addr & 0xFF]))
                for _ in range(args.frames):
                    frames.append(c.read_frame(expected_len=1)[0])
            except (ConsultError, TimeoutError) as e:
                c.t.note(f"sub {addr:04X} failed: {e}")
            finally:
                c.stop(timeout=0.5)
                c.t.drain(quiet=0.05)
            late = frames[len(frames) // 2:]
            ok = len(late) >= 2 and len(set(late)) == 1
            unstable += not ok

    def command(self, payload: bytes, retries=2):
        """Send a command list, check the echo, then send F0 to start streaming.

        The 1998 Maxima (seen 2026-11-14) sometimes answers a valid command with FE FE
        in place of the first echo pair, and sometimes echoes it correctly but answers
        F0 with FE and sends no frames. Both are retried after a stop.
        """
        want = expected_echo(payload)
        why = ""
        for n in range(retries + 1):
            got = self._send(payload, want)
            if got == want:
                self.t.write(bytes([GO]))
                first = self.t.read(1, timeout=0.5)
                if first == b"\xFF":
                    self._frame_started = True   # read_frame: FF already consumed
                    return
                why = f"F0 answered with {first.hex() or '(none)'}"
            else:
                why = f"bad echo {got.hex(' ') or '(none)'}, expected {want.hex(' ')}"
            self.t.note(f"command try {n + 1} failed: {why}")
            self.stop(timeout=0.5)
            self.t.drain(quiet=0.1)
        raise ConsultError(why)

    @property
    def paced(self):
        # The BCM (DA) answers FE to a command list sent in one burst, but accepts the
        # same bytes sent one at a time, each after its echo (2026-11-14).
        return getattr(self, "ecu", ENGINE) not in ENGINE_IDS

    def _send(self, payload, want):
        if not self.paced:
            self.t.write(payload)
            return self.t.read(len(want), timeout=0.5)
        got = bytearray()
        for i, b in enumerate(payload):
            self.t.write(bytes([b]))
            e = self.t.read(1, timeout=0.3)
            got += e
            if e != want[i:i + 1]:
                break
        return bytes(got)

    def read_frame(self, expected_len=None, timeout=1.0) -> bytes:
        """Read one FF <n> <data...> frame, parsing by length (data may contain FF)."""
        end = time.monotonic() + timeout
        while time.monotonic() < end:
            if getattr(self, "_frame_started", False):
                self._frame_started = False
            else:
                b = self.t.read(1, timeout=timeout)
                if not b:
                    break
                if b[0] != 0xFF:
                    continue
            n = self.t.read(1, timeout=0.3)
            if not n:
                break
            n = n[0]
            if expected_len is not None and n != expected_len:
                continue
            data = self.t.read(n, timeout=0.3)
            if len(data) == n:
                return data
        raise TimeoutError("no frame")

    def one_shot(self, payload: bytes, expected_len=None) -> bytes:
        """Command, read a single frame, stop."""
        self.command(payload)
        try:
            return self.read_frame(expected_len)
        finally:
            self.stop()

    def read_registers(self, regs):
        return b"".join(bytes([0x5A, r]) for r in regs)

    def part_number(self):
        d = self.one_shot(bytes([0xD0]))
        pn = None
        tail = d[-5:]
        engine = getattr(self, "ecu", ENGINE) in ENGINE_IDS
        if len(d) >= 5 and all(0x30 <= b < 0x5B for b in tail):

Now I understand the forward fully — and there's a real efficiency/reliability win to extract. The streaming loop (`$9B3F`) cycles through **all** queued forwarded addresses, one byte per frame. The current CLI pays a full command+stop handshake per single byte (1280 round-trips, each with a stale lead-in frame). Since `cs_argbuf` holds 20 C9 addresses, we can queue a whole block per request and let the ECU stream the block back — ~16× fewer handshakes and a coherent block per read. ## assistant 2026-11-15T19:16:37.109Z

Done. Here's what got squeezed out of the second-CPU forward:

**The tool now extracts the whole 1.25 KB window efficiently.** I rewrote `cmd_sub_dump` from one command-per-byte (1280 handshakes, each with a stale lead-in frame) to **block streaming**: it queues up to 20 C9 addresses per request — the `cs_argbuf` limit — and the ECU's streaming loop at `$9B3F` fills one payload slot per frame, cycling the queue. Default `--block 16` → ~80 requests instead of 1280, and each request returns a coherent block.

**The decode is proven correct and conservative.** I simulated the `$9B3F` streaming (stale-then-filled, cycling) and ran the real `_sub_block` against it: blocks of 1/6/16/20 all recover exactly, and under a deliberately stalled pipeline it flags unsettled slots `??` and **never reports a wrong byte as stable**. I can't touch the physical ECU from here, so that's validated against the ROM's behavior, not the car — the honest caveat is in the docs.

**What the window actually is.** The one block anyone's read, `rom/sub_0D40-0D4F` = `06 00 00 55 AA 00 …`. That `55 AA` is the knock interface chip's `AA55`/`55AA` self-test handshake from §8b — strong hint this slice is the **second CPU's knock/monitor RAM**, not its program. So the realistic prize here is live monitor state (the fault-detection flags `$0E51–$0E58` that set P0443 and misfire codes live on this CPU, §6), not its code. I set open-question 4 to watch those flags change as DTCs set.

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:23:50.837Z

Recorded as §11. This round was actually fruitful — a real bug plus the sharpest lead yet.

## What I found poking at `0A` direct mode

**1. A genuine firmware bug — integer underflow from a missing lower bound.**
Direct mode (`0A` with first byte `< $08`) computes a stream-table offset `(value − $80 − 1) × 4` on the high sub-paths. Each branch checks only the *upper* bound (e.g. `CMP #$84`), so `value = $80` slips through and underflows: `0 − 1 = $FF`, `×4 = $3FC`, low byte `$FC`. The handler then reads stream descriptors from `table_base + $FC` — way past the 16-byte table.

- Triggers: `0A <fb> 80` for `fb ∈ {0,2,5,6,7}`.
- `fb=0` self-rejects (OOB words are `0000`); the other four stream two bytes from unintended fixed ROM addresses (`$90F9/$A902`, etc.).
- The intended minimum was `value = $81` (offset 0). Classic off-by-one.
- **Access impact: none** — those are bank-0 bytes `C9` already returns. But it's a real input-validation defect, and it's read-only/safe to confirm on the car.

**2. The sharper discovery — a second read path with *no* hole check.**
`consult_reply_direct` (`$9CF1`) does `LDA $07A0,X; TAX; LDA $00,X`: it dereferences each `cs_streamlist` entry as an address and reads it **locally, in data bank 0, with none of the `$5D40–$623F` forward logic that `C9` applies.** So this engine is *strictly more permissive than `C9`* — an entry pointing into the hole would read this CPU's hidden code directly, no silicon needed.

Why it's not a win (yet): I scanned every descriptor table (`$E95F–$EA80`) and the OOB-bug targets — **none** points into `$5D40–$623F`, and `cs_streamlist` is never attacker-controlled; its entries only ever come from fixed ROM.

**But it reframes the whole hunt.** The target is no longer "defeat `C9`'s range check" (this path has none) — it's now one specific, concrete question: **is there any way to write a chosen 16-bit value into `$07A0`?** If such a primitive exists, this engine turns it into a hole-bypassing read of the hidden code. So far: no (active-test write stops at `$079C`, the `cs_argbuf` overflow reaches only `$08FA`). That's the sharpest remaining lead, and it's in §11.

I'll keep going if you like — next I'd sweep every RAM write whose destination is derived from a Consult byte, looking for one that can land on `$07A0–$07A3`. Or I can pause here and commit §6/§8c/§10/§11 + the sub-dump rewrite. Which way?

That closes the lead cleanly. Here's the result of the sweep you asked for.

## No write can land an attacker byte on `$07A0`

I enumerated every computed-destination store in the Consult path and traced each index:

| Write | Destination | Reaches `$07A0`? |
|---|---|---|
| `$50AF`, `$5103` (C9/5A arg) | `$08D2 + argc` | no — `$08Dx` |
| `$5152` (at_req) | `$07AC + (0..5)` | no — above it |
| `$519D` (**at_values**) | `$076F + at_slot` | **closest**, but caps at `$079C` |
| `$54A0`, `$54B2` (c9 hidden) | `$07C3+2n` / `$07D7+n` | no |
| `$9B5E` etc. (payload) | `$0740 + slot` | no |

Then I checked it from the other end — every store in the **whole image** that touches `$07A0–$07A3`. There are exactly three, and all write fixed ROM data (a table pointer, or words read from ROM, including the underflow source `table_base+$FC`). None copies a byte from the wire or from the attacker-controlled argument buffer.

The one indexed write that could be *bent* onto `$07A0` is the at_values store — it would need `at_slot = $31` (49). But `at_slot` is written at exactly one site (`$515F`), from the ROM descriptor, maxing at 45, and nowhere else — so it can't even be left stale-high across commands.

**So `cs_streamlist` is unconditionally fixed-content.** `consult_reply_direct`'s missing hole-check is real and architecturally interesting, but it's un-aimable from the Consult interface. Lead closed, recorded in §11.

## Where that leaves the whole audit

Every escalation shape is now swept and negative, each for a concrete reason:
- **Bank-crossing read** — DT is permanently 0, no long-indirect anywhere.
- **Arbitrary write** — every computed store is bounds-checked or fixed-destination; confirmed by the two-way sweep above.
- **Code execution** — only one indirect transfer, through a fixed ROM table.
- **The no-hole-check read path (`consult_reply_direct`)** — real, but its pointer source can't be influenced.
- **The two genuine bugs** (argbuf off-by-one, direct-mode underflow) — both land in dead RAM / fixed ROM.

That's a thorough negative: the Consult interface genuinely cannot be made to exceed `C9`'s reach in software. Bank 1 and the `$5D40–$623F` code stay silicon-only (§8c).

I've got a solid docs set now (§6, §8c, §10, §11) plus the sub-dump rewrite, all unstaged on `main`. Want me to branch and commit it? I can keep hunting other corners too (e.g. the second-CPU message parser `$C7F5`, or a correctness pass on our own Python/C tools), but the access-escalation question is answered.

def decode(names, data):
    """Turn a frame (in request order) into {name: (value, unit)}."""
    out, i = {}, 0
    for name in names:
        regs, fn, unit = ENGINE[name]
        raw = 0
        for b in data[i:i + len(regs)]:
            raw = (raw << 8) | b
        out[name] = (fn(raw), unit)
        i += len(regs)
    return out


def registers_for(names):
    return [r for name in names for r in ENGINE[name][0]]

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:30:45.920Z

Two concrete, actionable bugs in our own code this round:

## Bug 1 — `decode()` silently mis-scales malformed frames (consult/registers.py)

`decode()` has no length check. The demo above shows the failure modes on a 9600-baud line that drops or gains a byte:

- **One byte short:** the truncated register silently reads `0` (`tps: (0, 'mV')`) — a plausible-looking value, not an error.
- **One byte of desync** (extra leading byte): *every* register shifts and silently returns garbage that often looks real (`coolant: (-50 °C)`, `tps: (2440 mV)`).

It just consumes `data[i:i+len(regs)]`, pads missing bytes with nothing, and advances `i` regardless. So a single serial glitch produces wrong readings on `watch`/`snapshot` with no indication. Fix is a one-liner: verify `len(data) == sum(len(regs) …)` and raise/flag otherwise.

## Bug 2 — O2 (and L/R) bank labels assert a mapping the project marks "open"

`CAR_TEST_CHECKLIST.md:61` says of registers `09`/`0A`: **"Which bank is which: open."** But `registers.py` *and* `registers.c` both hardcode `09 = "O2 sensor LH"`, `0A = "O2 sensor RH"` as settled fact. And `ROM_ANALYSIS.md` §2 notes the FSM convention is **B1 = right, B2 = left** — with nothing pinning register `09` to B1 or B2. So:

- If `09 = B1 = right`, the `LH`/`RH` labels are **swapped**.
- The same unverified L/R assumption rides along on `inj_lh/rh` (14/15 vs 22/23), `alpha_lh/rh`, and `learn_lh/rh`.

This isn't a scaling error — the C and Python scalings agree perfectly — it's a labeling claim that contradicts the team's own open question. Every "LH/RH" reading could be reversed. It needs car verification (induce a known single-bank condition, or read a bank-specific DTC's freeze frame), or the names should be made provisional (e.g. `o2_09`/`o2_0A`) until then.

---

Firmware side this round was clean except one trivial off-by-one: the DTC reply cap (`$9A90`) checks *after* writing, so a 21st stored code writes 2 bytes into unused padding (`$0768–$0769`) — harmless, not Consult-triggerable. The second-CPU message parser is a flat fixed-offset copy with no bounds exposure.

Want me to fix Bug 1 (add the length guard to `decode()`) and reword the O2/fuel L/R labels to provisional in both `registers.py` and `registers.c`? And I can keep going into `src/gui.c` and the disassembler next.

int consult_read_frame(consult_t *c, int expected_len, double timeout, uint8_t *out)
{
    double end = mono() + timeout;
    while (mono() < end && !cancelled(c) && !c->s->error) {
        uint8_t b, n;
        if (c->frame_started) {
            c->frame_started = 0;
        } else {
            if (serial_read(c->s, &b, 1, timeout) != 1)
                break;
            if (b != 0xFF)
                continue;
        }
        if (serial_read(c->s, &n, 1, 0.3) != 1)
            break;
        if (expected_len >= 0 && n != expected_len)
            continue;
        if (serial_read(c->s, out, n, 0.3) == n)
            return n;
    }
    snprintf(c->err, sizeof c->err, "no frame");
    return -1;
}

    consult_stop(c, 2.0, NULL);
    return len;
}

int consult_dtcs(consult_t *c, consult_dtc_t *out, int max)
{
    const uint8_t cmd = 0xD1;
    uint8_t d[CONSULT_MAX_FRAME];
    int n = consult_one_shot(c, &cmd, 1, d), k = 0;

    if (n < 0)
        return -1;
    for (int i = 0; i + 1 < n && k < max; i += 2, k++) {
        out[k].code = d[i];
        out[k].starts = d[i + 1];
    }
    return k;
}

int consult_read_memory(consult_t *c, const uint16_t *addrs, int n, uint8_t *out)
{
    uint8_t payload[3 * 8], d[CONSULT_MAX_FRAME];
    int len;

    if (n < 1 || n > 8) {
        snprintf(c->err, sizeof c->err, "C9 takes 1..8 addresses");
        return 0;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        payload[3 * i] = 0xC9;
        payload[3 * i + 1] = addrs[i] >> 8;
        payload[3 * i + 2] = addrs[i] & 0xFF;
    }
    len = consult_one_shot(c, payload, 3 * (size_t)n, d);
    if (len != n) {
        if (len >= 0)
            snprintf(c->err, sizeof c->err, "C9 frame of %d bytes, expected %d", len, n);
        return 0;
    }

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:38:06.578Z

Confirmed root cause. Here's the real bug:

## Confirmed disassembler bug: subroutine flag mis-track loses real code

`JSL $5531` **returns with m=1** (its last width op before returning is `SEM` at `$556F`; it was entered after the caller's `CLM` at `$40A9`). But the walker's documented assumption is "a subroutine returns with the flags it was called with," so it continues the caller at `$40B4` with **m=0**. The mismatch is invisible until the first m-width-dependent operand — the `BBS` at `$40C0`:

| | Walker (m=0, wrong) | Reality (m=1) |
|---|---|---|
| `$40C0` | `BBS $0211,#$0302,L_4053` (6 B) — target **mid-instruction**, nonsense mask | `BBS $0211,#$02,L_40C8` (5 B) — **clean target** |
| `$40C5` | — | `STA $0E4C` |
| `$40C6` | `JMP L_1C0E` (into a **data table**) | — |
| `$40C9+` | **marked as `.db` data** | real code (`CLB $07F6,#$02`, `JSL $0101D0`, …) |

The wide mis-decode makes `$40C0` end at `$40C6`, which decodes as an unconditional `JMP`, so the walker **stops** — and **~100+ bytes of real code at `$40C9–$412x` are silently mis-labeled as data.** The `$8AD0–$8AEA` cluster is the same class (mis-decoded region resyncing at real code `$8AEB`).

So the "A subroutine returns with the flags it was called with" assumption in the docstring is **not always true in this ROM** — `$5531` is a counterexample — and where it breaks, it doesn't just garble one instruction, it drops a whole code tail into the data bucket.

**Impact on the project:** any `ROM_ANALYSIS.md` claim about code in `$40C9–$412x` or `$8AD0–$8AEA` is unreliable, and there may be other such spots wherever a flag-changing subroutine is called in a 16-bit context. The 5-target boundary check is a good detector — it flagged exactly these.

Let me check whether the annotation file can already force flags at an address (the clean fix), or whether that mechanism needs adding.

ram 00F1 sio_rxctl    Consult RX enable (low 3 bits)

    """Hand annotations for one ROM, read from a text file. One directive per line:

        ram   ADDR name  [description]   name a RAM/IO address (used in operand comments)
        label ADDR name                  name a code or data address
        head  ADDR text                  comment line(s) printed before ADDR ("-" = file header)
        note  ADDR text                  comment at the end of the line at ADDR
        table ADDR SIZE name  description   data block printed as a named table
        hole  ADDR SIZE text             bytes in the image that aren't real ROM: never decoded

    ADDR and SIZE are hex. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.ram, self.ram_desc, self.labels, self.notes, self.tables = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
        self.heads = collections.defaultdict(list)
        self.holes = []

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path):
        a = cls()
        for n, line in enumerate(open(path, encoding="utf-8"), 1):
            line = line.rstrip("\n")
            if not line.strip() or line.lstrip().startswith("#"):
                continue
            kind, rest = (line.split(None, 1) + [""])[:2]
            try:
                if kind == "head":
                    addr, _, text = rest.partition(" ")
                    a.heads[-1 if addr == "-" else int(addr, 16)].append(text.strip())
                    continue
                addr_s, _, rest = rest.partition(" ")
                addr, rest = int(addr_s, 16), rest.strip()
                if kind == "ram":
                    name, _, desc = rest.partition(" ")
                    a.ram[addr], a.ram_desc[addr] = name, desc.strip()
                elif kind == "label":
                    a.labels[addr] = rest
                elif kind == "note":
                    a.notes[addr] = rest
                elif kind == "hole":
                    size_s, _, why = rest.partition(" ")
                    a.holes.append((addr, addr + int(size_s, 16), why.strip()))
                elif kind == "table":
                    size_s, name, desc = (rest.split(None, 2) + [""])[:3]
                    a.tables[addr] = (name, desc, int(size_s, 16))
                else:
                    raise ValueError(f"unknown directive '{kind}'")
            except ValueError as e:
                sys.exit(f"{path}:{n}: {e}")
        return a

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:39:01.446Z

Disassembler audit complete. This was the most productive target — I found a **confirmed bug that silently loses real code**.

## The bug

The docstring's core assumption — "a subroutine returns with the flags it was called with" — is **false for at least one routine in this ROM**. `JSL $5531` returns with `m=1` (8-bit), but the walker continues the caller at `$40B4` with the `m=0` it had before the call. The mismatch is invisible until the first m-width-dependent operand, the `BBS` at `$40C0`:

- **Walker (m=0):** decodes it 6 bytes wide → bogus mask `#$0302`, target `$4053` landing mid-instruction, then a phantom `JMP` into a data table, then **stops** — marking `$40C9–$412x` as `.db` data.
- **Reality (m=1):** `BBS $0211,#$02,L_40C8` (5 bytes, clean target) → `STA $0E4C` → real code continues.

So ~100+ bytes of a real function tail are mislabeled as data. The `$8AD0–$8AEA` cluster is the same failure mode.

## How I found it (reusable regression test)

I parsed the listing and checked the invariant **every branch/jump/call target must land on an instruction start**. 2833/2838 passed; the 5 failures were: 3 benign (one external RAM target `$0400`, two in the documented `$5D40–$623F` hole) and **2 real** (`$40C0`, `$8AD0`). That boundary check is worth keeping as a post-rebuild test.

## Also found

- **Docstring was inaccurate** — it claimed PHP/PLP tracking that doesn't exist in the code. I corrected it. (It turns out harmless here: this ROM only uses PHP/PLP to save condition flags, never to wrap a width change — I verified the sites.)
- **Latent soundness gaps**, now documented in the docstring: first-path-wins decides m/x (later paths with different width are ignored), and the subroutine-flag assumption.
- Minor precision issues: a couple of data regions (`$1BAC`, `$1C00` table area) decoded as code via jump-table/target over-reach.

## Impact & fix

Any `ROM_ANALYSIS.md` claim about code in `$40C9–$412x` or `$8AD0–$8AEA` is unreliable (those bytes are mislabeled). The clean fix: add a `code ADDR [m x]` annotation directive that seeds the walker at a given address with forced flags, then annotate the known-bad spots to recover the lost code. I've recorded the offenders and the fix direction in the docstring.

Want me to implement that `code` seed directive + the boundary-check as a test script, and recover the `$40C9` code tail? That's a real improvement to the tool everything else depends on. Otherwise I can keep hunting other regions (re-run the detector is the fast way to find any more).

def format_table(rom, addr, ann, out):
    """Emit an annotated data table."""
    name, desc, size = ann
    out.write(f"\n; === {name}: {desc} ===\n")
    if size == 256 and "16x16" in desc:
        out.write(f"{name}:  ; ${addr:04X}\n")
        out.write(f";       col: {'  '.join(f'{c:X}' for c in range(16))}\n")
        for row in range(16):
            cells = [rom.r8(addr + row * 16 + c) for c in range(16)]
            hex_part = " ".join(f"{v:02X}" for v in cells)
            out.write(f";  row {row:X}:  {hex_part}\n")
        for off in range(0, 256, 16):
            row_addr = addr + off
            vals = [rom.r8(row_addr + j) for j in range(16)]
            hex_str = " ".join(f"{v:02X}" for v in vals)
            out.write(f"    {row_addr:04X}  {hex_str}\n")
            out.write(f"          .db {','.join(f'${v:02X}' for v in vals)}\n")
    elif "1D lookup" in desc:
        n = size
        vals = [rom.r8(addr + k) for k in range(n)]
        out.write(f"{name}:  ; ${addr:04X}, {n} bytes\n")
        out.write(f";  values: {' '.join(f'{v:02X}' for v in vals)}\n")
        hex_str = " ".join(f"{v:02X}" for v in vals)
        out.write(f"    {addr:04X}  {hex_str}\n")
        out.write(f"          .db {','.join(f'${v:02X}' for v in vals)}\n")
    else:
        out.write(f"{name}:  ; ${addr:04X}, {size} bytes\n")
        for off in range(0, size, 16):
            row_addr = addr + off
            n = min(16, size - off)
            vals = [rom.r8(row_addr + j) for j in range(n)]
            hex_str = " ".join(f"{v:02X}" for v in vals)
            out.write(f"    {row_addr:04X}  {hex_str}\n")
            out.write(f"          .db {','.join(f'${v:02X}' for v in vals)}\n")


def format_listing(rom, insns, labels, annotations, out, ann, title):
    out.write(f"; M7700 disassembly — {title}\n")

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="M7700 recursive-descent disassembler")
    parser.add_argument("rom", help="Binary ROM image")
    parser.add_argument("--base", type=lambda x: int(x, 16), default=0x1000,
                        help="Load address in hex (default: 1000)")
    parser.add_argument("--ann", help="Annotation file (see Ann)")
    parser.add_argument("--title", help="Listing title (default: ROM file name)")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", help="Output file (default: stdout)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(args.rom, "rb") as f:
        data = f.read()
    rom = Rom(data, args.base)
    print(f"Loaded {len(data)} bytes at ${args.base:04X}-${rom.end - 1:04X}", file=sys.stderr)

    ann = Ann.load(args.ann) if args.ann else Ann()
    SENSOR_NAMES.update(ann.ram)
    rom.holes = ann.holes
    title = args.title or os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(args.rom))[0]

    insns, labels = walk(rom)
    print(f"Decoded {len(insns)} instructions, {len(labels)} labels", file=sys.stderr)

    annotations = find_tables(rom, insns)
    # Hand-named tables win; drop generated tables that overlap them.
    for ta, (name, desc, size) in ann.tables.items():
        for other in [o for o, a in annotations.items() if o < ta + size and ta < o + a[2]]:
            del annotations[other]
        annotations[ta] = (name, desc, size)
    print(f"Found {len(annotations)} annotated tables", file=sys.stderr)

    if args.output:
        with open(args.output, "w") as f:
            format_listing(rom, insns, labels, annotations, f, ann, title)
        print(f"Wrote {args.output}", file=sys.stderr)
    else:
        format_listing(rom, insns, labels, annotations, sys.stdout, ann, title)

  "file_path": "/home/emma/Documents/GitHub/open-consult/tools/check_targets.py",
  "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Sanity-check a m7700dis.py listing: every branch/jump/call target must land on an\ninstruction boundary. A target in the middle of an instruction means the decoder\nmis-sized something earlier (usually an m/x flag mis-track), so the rest of that block\nis wrong. See the KNOWN MIS-DECODES note in m7700dis.py; the fix is a `code ADDR m x`\nseed in the .ann.\n\n    python3 tools/check_targets.py rom/23710-2L904.asm\n\nExits non-zero if any target is off-boundary, ignoring targets below the image base\n(external/RAM) and inside declared holes (printed as data, never disassembled).\n\"\"\"\nimport re\nimport sys\n\n\ndef main():\n    if len(sys.argv) != 2:\n        sys.exit(\"usage: check_targets.py LISTING.asm\")\n    lines = open(sys.argv[1], encoding=\"utf-8\").read().splitlines()\n    addr_re = re.compile(r\"^\\s{4}([0-9A-F]{4})  \")\n\n    starts, datalines, base = set(), set(), None\n    for line in lines:\n        m = addr_re.match(line)\n        if not m:\n            continue\n        a = int(m.group(1), 16)\n        base = a if base is None else min(base, a)\n        (datalines if \".db \" in line else starts).add(a)\n\n    refs = {int(t, 16) for line in lines for t in re.findall(r\"L_([0-9A-F]{4})\", line)}\n    bad = [a for a in sorted(refs)\n           if a not in starts and a >= (base or 0) and a not in datalines]\n\n    print(f\"{len(starts)} instruction starts, {len(refs)} targets, {len(bad)} off-boundary\")\n    for a in bad:\n        print(f\"  L_{a:04X} lands mid-instruction or in data (likely a flag mis-track \"\n              f\"earlier; add a `code {a:04X} m x` seed)\")\n    return 1 if bad else 0\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    sys.exit(main())\n"
}
````

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:43:34.760Z

The disassembler bug is fixed and verified. The checker now exits **0** — every one of 2862 control-flow targets lands on an instruction boundary.

## What I changed

1. **`tools/m7700dis.py`** — added a `code ADDR [m x]` annotation directive that seeds a walk at a given address with forced m/x flags, processed *before* the vector walk so it claims those addresses before a mis-tracked fall-through can decode them at the wrong width. Also corrected the docstring (removed the false "PHP/PLP tracked" claim, documented the two soundness assumptions and the known failure mode + detector).

2. **`rom/23710-2L904.ann`** — two surgical seeds:
   - `code 40C0 1 0` — `JSL $5531` returns `m=1`; recovers the `$40C9–$412x` code tail that was dropped into data.
   - `code 8AD8 0 0` — reached first at `m=1` by another path; the `CLM` at `$8AD3` makes it `m=0`.

3. **`rom/23710-2L904.asm`** — regenerated: **+259 instructions recovered** (15926 → 16185), the two code tails now decode as real code, and the `$1BAC` data-as-code phantom vanished (it was downstream of the cascade).

4. **`tools/check_targets.py`** (new) — the regression test: parses a listing, asserts every branch/jump/call target hits an instruction start, and exits non-zero otherwise. Hole-aware and base-aware, so a clean listing passes. This is the oracle that found the bug, now reusable after every rebuild.

## Verification

- All 5 originally mis-decoded targets resolve; the recovered code is sensible (`BBS $0211,#$02,L_40C8` → `STA $0E4C` → `JSL $0101D0` …).
- `check_targets.py` exits 0 (only the 3 genuinely-external targets — below-base and in-hole — remain, all correctly exempted).

The fix is reproducible with the documented regenerate command, and the root-cause assumptions are now written down so the next person hits the detector, not a silent gap.

One caveat worth flagging: the `$5531`-returns-`m=1` case means **other** flag-changing subroutines called in 16-bit contexts could have the same latent issue in regions that happen not to have a branch target landing mid-instruction (so the detector wouldn't catch them). The detector catches the *symptomatic* ones, which is most. If you want belt-and-suspenders, the fuller fix is modeling subroutine exit flags via a fixpoint — bigger change, probably not worth it given how few sites exist.

This whole session's work (sub-dump rewrite, ROM_ANALYSIS §6/§8c/§10/§11, the disassembler fix + test) is unstaged on `main`. Want me to branch and commit it?

## assistant 2026-11-15T19:45:40.811Z

{
  "command": "python3 -I - <<'EOF'\n# Find loops of the shape: STA/STB $00,X (or abs,X) ; ... ; INX ; CPX #imm ; BCC/BCS back\n# i.e. a store into an indexed buffer whose end is tested. Flag ones where the compare\n# is AFTER the store with no pre-store guard (off-by-one risk like the DTC reply).\nimport re\nlines=open(\"rom/23710-2L904.asm\").read().splitlines()\ninsn=re.compile(r\"^\\s{4}([0-9A-F]{4})  (?:[0-9A-F]{2} )+\\s*([A-Z]{2,4})\\b(.*)$\")\nrows=[]\nfor L in lines:\n    m=insn.match(L)\n    if m: rows.append((int(m.group(1),16), m.group(2), m.group(3).strip()))\n# scan windows for store-then-compare-then-backbranch\nhits=0\nfor i,(a,op,arg) in enumerate(rows):\n    if op not in (\"STA\",\"STB\"): continue\n    if \",X\" not in arg and \",Y\" not in arg: continue\n    # look ahead up to 8 insns for CPX/CPY #imm then a conditional back-branch to <= a\n    for j in range(i+1, min(i+9,len(rows))):\n        aj,opj,argj=rows[j]\n        if opj in (\"CPX\",\"CPY\") and argj.startswith(\"#$\"):\n            # find the branch after the compare\n            for k in range(j+1,min(j+3,len(rows))):\n                ak,opk,argk=rows[k]\n                if opk in (\"BCC\",\"BCS\",\"BNE\",\"BEQ\"):\n                    tgt=re.search(r\"L_([0-9A-F]{4})\",argk)\n                    if tgt and int(tgt.group(1),16)<=a:   # back-branch = loop\n                        hits+=1\n                        print(f\"{a:04X} {op}{arg:>14}  ->  {aj:04X} {opj} {argj}  {ak:04X} {opk} {argk}\")\n                    break\n            break\nprint(\"candidate store-then-check loops:\",hits)\nEOF",
  "description": "Sweep for post-store bound-check off-by-one loops"
}
````

## A genuine lead worth flagging — possible knock OOB-by-one

This is the one thing that isn't a clean "correct." In `isr_tb2`, the cylinder index for the knock table is computed as `(0A0D + 1) & $0F` **with no wrap at 6**, then used to index the 6-word table at `$0DE1`. If `$0A0D` reaches 5 at that read, `+1 = 6` → it reads `$0DED` (a *different* knock variable, confirmed used elsewhere at `$414C`/`$A3B2`) one word past the table and writes it to the knock chip as that cylinder's detection window.

I was **honest in the annotation that I couldn't confirm it**: whether `$0A0D` actually hits 5 at the Timer-B2 read depends on the crank-angle cylinder sequencing, which I didn't fully trace. So it's recorded as "OOB-by-one IF `$0A0D` hits 5 — unconfirmed, worth checking," not asserted as a bug. `isr_ta4` reads `$0A0D` without the `+1`, so it's only the B2 path at risk. If real, the effect is a mis-set knock window once per cycle (minor, which fits code that's run fine for decades).

To confirm/refute it properly I'd need to trace the POS/REF interrupt that sequences `$0A0D` (counter at `$48B1`, reset condition at `$48B4`) and establish its range at the B2 firing point — a deeper trace I can do next if you want it nailed down.

Resolved. The decisive facts:

1. **`$0A07` is the real 0–5 cylinder counter** (`$4A41 INA; CMP #$06; BCC; LDA #$00` — explicit wrap at 6), not `$0A0D`.
2. **`STA $0A0C` at `$4A5A` is an 8-bit store** (after `$4A54 SEM`), so it writes only `$0A0C` — it does **not** clobber `$0A0D`.
3. **`$0A0D` is maintained solely at `$48B1`** (`m=1` confirmed: `SEM` at `$4860` with no intervening `CLM`): `INC`, then clear the low 7 bits whenever `$0A0D & $06 ≠ 0`. Simulating: `0→1` (keeps), `1→2` (`2&6≠0` → clears). So between passes the low nibble is **only ever {0, 1}**.

So the knock index `($0A0D [+1]) & $0F` ∈ {0,1,2}, reading `$0DE1/$0DE3/$0DE5` — comfortably inside the table. **There is no out-of-bounds read.** My earlier flag was a false alarm: I'd assumed `$0A0D` was the cylinder index, but it's actually a 0/1 toggle (likely a double-buffer select for the knock window), and the cylinder counter is `$0A07`.

Let me correct the annotation to record the resolution.

Good instinct — that's exactly the right lever to lean on. The primitive is `consult_reply_direct` (`$9CF1`): it takes each `cs_streamlist` entry, treats it as an address, and streams `mem[addr]` back to us **with no `$5D40–$623F` hole check and no forward** — so unlike `C9`, if an entry points into the hole it reads *this* CPU's hidden code locally. And yes, we can fire `0A <fb> <value>` as many times as we like.

The whole question reduces to: **can any reachable `(fb, value)` put a hole address (`$5D40–$623F`) into `cs_streamlist`?** The entries are fixed ROM descriptor words, but I only spot-checked a few earlier. Let me exhaustively enumerate every accepted `(fb, value)`, compute its exact offset (including the `0x80` underflow), read the two entry words, and flag anything that dereferences into the hole — or anywhere else we can't already reach.

1. **The config bits are immutable.** Every one of the ~25 references to `$1206`/`$1207` is a direct `BBC/BBS $12xx` read testing the bit in place — **none copies either byte to RAM**.
